p: Long called "la Savane", then place de l'Esplanade, the square was laid out from 1821. It is now a listed historic monument, together with its fittings, statues and street furniture.
Its palms are royal palms (Roystonea oleacea), native to Venezuela and the southern Caribbean. In 1995, 296 remained and 202 spots were empty: replanting explains why the trees differ in height.

At the centre stands the monument to Félix Éboué, unveiled in 1957. Born in Cayenne, he was a colonial governor and a leading figure of Free France, and rests in the Panthéon. The statue replaced a fountain dedicated to mayor Nicolas Merlet.

Around the square are some of the city's finest Creole houses, including the Thémire house, home since 1908 to the Hôtel and Bar des Palmistes, and the Franconie building, seat of the departmental museum.
In the evening, food trucks bring the square to life. It is the natural start of a walk through the old town: Fort Cépérou is about 700 metres away, the market a few streets off.

faq.a: For the hundreds of royal palms planted on the square, a species from Venezuela and the southern Caribbean.

faq.q: Who is the statue in the middle?
faq.a: Félix Éboué, born in Cayenne, governor and figure of Free France. The monument dates from 1957.

faq.q: Is the square lively at night?
faq.a: Yes: food trucks set up in the evening and locals meet there.

p: In 1643, Charles Poncet de Brétigny acquired the hill above the mouth of the Cayenne River from a Kali'na chief, Cépérou (Sépélu in Amerindian accounts), who gave it his name. A first wooden fort was built there: this is the founding of Cayenne, which grew at the foot of its walls.
The fort was successively named Saint-Michel and Saint-Louis before taking back the name Cépérou. In 1676, Dutch admiral Jacob Binckes landed 900 men nearby and the garrison surrendered.
Little remains of the fort itself: a vaulted passage, some walls and the hilltop. But the view, 28 metres above the sea, takes in the city roofs, the estuary and the ocean.
The climb is short, up a few steps. The site is about 700 metres from Place des Palmistes; go in the late afternoon for the light and the cooler air.

faq.q: Where does the name Cépérou come from?
faq.a: From a Kali'na chief who ceded the hill to the French around 1643.

faq.q: What is left of the fort?
faq.a: Not much: a vaulted passage and sections of wall. People come mainly for the view.
Yes, the site is open access.

p: In 1907, the town council decided to build a covered hall with a metal frame; it opened in 1910. Today it is the largest market in French Guiana.

Outside, stalls of local fruit and vegetables: rambutans, yams, chillies, herbs. Under the hall, butchers, spices, Amerindian and Maroon crafts, and above all the phở soup counters run by Hmong families, a local breakfast ritual.

The market runs on Wednesday, Friday and Saturday mornings, on Place du Coq. Come early: it starts at dawn and winds down in the early afternoon. Saturday is the busiest day. Bring cash for small stalls.

faq.q: Which days is Cayenne market open?
faq.a: Wednesday, Friday and Saturday mornings. Exact hours vary between sources: come early.
Hmong phở soup is the institution, along with fresh juices and accras.
Decided in 1907, it opened in 1910.

p: Founded in 1995, the Museum of Guianese Cultures preserves and presents objects from the peoples who built French Guiana: Amerindians, Bushinengue, Creoles, and more recent communities such as Hmong, Brazilians and Haitians. It manages about 10,000 objects, plus archaeological collections, images and sound archives.

The museum occupies two houses on rue Madame-Payé, at numbers 54 and 78. One is a Creole house built in 1870 by a family of gold miners, a fine example of traditional architecture. Two to three temporary exhibitions a year rotate the collections, on themes such as Maroon textiles or tembé art.
Opening hours vary by day and it is usually closed at weekends in the afternoon: check before you go. Workshops run during the short school holidays.

faq.a: At 54 and 78 rue Madame-Payé, in central Cayenne.
Objects, images and sounds from Amerindian, Bushinengue and Creole cultures and from more recent communities.
Yes, workshops during the short school holidays.

p: The Franconie building belonged to a family settled in French Guiana since the 17th century. The administration bought it in 1885 from deputy Gustave Franconie, who donated his father Alexandre's library. The museum, one of the oldest cultural institutions in French Guiana, opened there in 1901.
The house has been a listed historic monument since 1986 and bears the "Maison des Illustres" label.

A true cabinet of curiosities: natural history, archaeology, Amerindian, Bushinengue and Creole ethnography, minerals. Highlights include Father Yves Barbotin's insect collection of nearly 4,000 specimens, the penal colony scenes painted by former convict Francis Lagrange, and the memory of Félix Éboué.
The museum faces Place des Palmistes. It opens mostly on weekday mornings, with two afternoons: check opening hours before you go.

faq.a: It opened in 1901, in the building acquired by the colony in 1885.
Francis Lagrange's penal colony paintings and Father Barbotin's insect collection.
1 avenue du Général-de-Gaulle, on Place des Palmistes.

p: The beaches of Rémire-Montjoly and Cayenne are among French Guiana's major nesting sites. You mostly see the leatherback, a giant up to 2 metres long and about 400 kg, and the olive ridley; more rarely the green and hawksbill turtles.

Nesting runs from April to August, and hatchlings emerge for weeks after. The Kwata association has monitored these populations for more than 25 years and runs information patrols on the beach during the season.

A long sandy beach lined with coconut palms. The water is brown: it carries Amazon sediment swept along the coast by the current. The Guianese coastline moves fast, and strong April and May tides can push the beach back.
To watch nesting: no white light or flash, stay behind the turtle and keep your distance, let hatchlings reach the sea. Dogs are banned on the beach and at the nearby Salines.

faq.q: When can I see turtles at Montjoly?
faq.a: April to August for nesting, with a leatherback peak in May and June; hatchlings follow in summer.
With care: ask locally about currents and sea conditions.
Because of Amazon sediment carried along the coast by the current.

p: A former saltworks, these 63 hectares belong to the Conservatoire du littoral, which bought the first plots in 1981. The site has been protected since 1985 and managed by the Kwata association since 2012, with the town of Rémire-Montjoly.
The trail crosses four habitats in a short distance: the beach and its mudflats, the dune ridge and its coastal forest, the mangrove, then the marsh.
A boardwalk on stilts crosses the red mangrove, and a shelter overlooks the marsh for birdwatching. It is one of the few mangroves in French Guiana you can explore on foot.
The trail is about 2.5 km and easy; it starts at the end of chemin Saint-Dominique, behind Montjoly beach. Go early: the sand heats up fast. Dogs are not allowed.

faq.q: How long is the Salines trail?
faq.a: About 2.5 km, easy.
The Conservatoire du littoral owns it; the Kwata association manages it with the town.
Marsh and shore birds, mangrove crabs, sometimes mammals at dawn.

p: The Rorota trail is a 5.6 km loop on Mahury mountain, in Rémire-Montjoly. Easy to moderate, with about 150 metres of climbing, it is one of the busiest hikes on Cayenne island and a good first taste of the forest.

The path skirts three reservoirs, the Rorota, Lalouette and Rémire lakes, which supply the area with drinking water. A viewpoint opens over Gosselin cove and Montravel hill. With luck and silence, sloths and monkeys show up in the trees.
Start from the beach road, at the signposted turn after the old distillery; parking at the trailhead by Lake Saccharin. Allow 1 h 30 to 2 h. Start early and carry water.

faq.q: How long is the Rorota trail?
faq.a: A 5.6 km loop, about 150 m of climbing, 1 h 30 to 2 h.

faq.q: Can I swim in the lakes?
faq.a: They are drinking-water reservoirs: swimming is not intended there.
Sloths, monkeys and many birds, especially early in the morning.

p: The Jesuits founded the Loyola estate in 1668 in Rémire, about ten kilometres from Cayenne. It became a sugar plantation, then the largest slave plantation in French Guiana: over 1,000 hectares and about 500 enslaved people, with the fathers' house, chapel, cemetery, forge, hospital, sugar works and indigo works.
Around 1740, the Jesuits gave up sugar and moved the equipment to Saint-Régis. After the Society of Jesus was banned in 1763, the estate was abandoned.

The trail crosses the terraces and stone remains of the estate, excavated since the 1990s by archaeologists including a team from Université Laval. The 1733 windmill, a listed monument, can now be seen from the Rémire road. The remains have been listed since 1993.
This is a place of memory of slavery as much as an archaeological site. The trail combines easily with the Rorota or Vidal trails.

faq.a: The Jesuits, in 1668.
Over 1,000 hectares and about 500 enslaved people at its peak.
Terraces, stone walls and the 1733 windmill.

p: From the 17th century, the first settlers fortified this point at the mouth of the Mahury, the gateway to Cayenne island. The present fort is a coastal battery built in the 1840s and completed around 1849. It has been a listed historic monument since 1980 and belongs to the department.

The plan is unusual: a half-moon battery facing the ocean, a casemated traverse of nine cells, and a V-shaped redan pointing towards Mount Mahury. The walls, about two metres thick, combine basalt and brick. The grassy slope was meant to hide the fort from ships at sea.
The interior is usually open only during European Heritage Days; the rest of the year, admire it from outside, with the view over the estuary.

faq.q: Can I visit inside Fort Diamant?
faq.a: Usually only during European Heritage Days.
The present fort dates from the 1840s, on a site fortified since the 17th century.
The origin is debated: it is often linked to its shape, or to a nearby landing that already bore the name in the 18th century.

p: Mont Bourda is a small forested massif of about thirty hectares rising to 114 metres, between Cayenne and Rémire-Montjoly. It is managed by the Conservatoire du littoral and is part of the trail network linking Montabo hill to Bourda, about 3.8 km long.
The path climbs through the undergrowth to the calvary at the top. The view over Salines beach used to be open; vegetation has partly closed it, but glimpses of the sea remain along the way.
Access via route de Montabo, then route de Bourda; parking near the trailhead sign. The trail is busy with local joggers in the late afternoon: go with company and bring a torch if you start late.

faq.a: About 114 metres.
One to two hours depending on the loop; the Montabo–Bourda link is about 3.8 km.

faq.q: Is there a view at the top?
faq.a: The summit calvary is partly surrounded by vegetation; the best sea views are along the way.

p: The Mont Grand Matoury national nature reserve was created by decree on 6 September 2006 and covers about 2,123 hectares. It is France's largest peri-urban nature reserve: real tropical forest in the heart of Cayenne island, with a summit at 254 metres.

The La Mirande trails offer three routes: the grand tour (3.9 km, about 4 h), the waterfall loop (2.5 km, about 2 h) and the Paypayo loop (2 km, about 1 h 30). Another trail, the Lac des Américains path, crosses one of the last fragments of primary forest on the coast.
The reserve is above all rich in birds: get up early to hear them. Stay on the marked trails and leave plants be: everything here is protected.

faq.q: Since when is Mont Grand Matoury a reserve?
faq.a: Since the decree of 6 September 2006.
The Paypayo loop (2 km) for a first visit, the grand tour (3.9 km) for half a day.
254 metres.

p: Two walks share Montabo hill, north-east of Cayenne. The coastal trail, easy and well marked, runs along the sea and ends on an often deserted beach. The hill trail, about 3.8 km and waymarked, goes into dense, well-preserved forest a few minutes from downtown; allow 2 to 2 h 30.
The route alternates shaded stretches and views over the Atlantic. Cayenne's coastline, lined with mangroves and mudflats, is good for watching migratory birds, from Pointe Buzaré to Anse Chaton.
The hill trail starts on route de Montabo, behind the IRD. Several Montabo beaches are supervised bathing sites: follow the signs and beware of currents and mudbanks.

faq.a: No: the coastal trail is easy, and so is the waymarked hill trail, about 3.8 km.
On route de Montabo, behind the IRD.
On Montabo's supervised beaches, following the posted instructions.

p: The Vidal estate, also called Mondélice, was a sugar plantation worked by enslaved people at the foot of the Mahury plateau. In 1819 it was described as "newly set up as a sugar works", with new buildings and mills and copper boilers. The estate has been abandoned since 1880.

Its remains were listed as a historic monument in 1999. The site, owned by the Conservatoire du littoral since 2015 and protected as a landscape in 2016, has been managed by the Kwata association since 2020.

A forest path of nearly 3 km leads to the ruins of the sugar works and its machinery, overgrown by vegetation. Along the way, the secondary forest is rich in birds: black-necked aracaris, channel-billed toucans, hermits, potoos.
The start is poorly signposted, between the stadium and the Léon-Gontran-Damas high school. Kwata runs themed outings (history, ethnobotany, biodiversity).

faq.a: A slave sugar plantation, set up in the early 19th century and abandoned around 1880.
Nearly 3 km to the remains.
The Kwata association, for the Conservatoire du littoral.

p: The Montagne Topu trail, managed by the Collectivité territoriale de Guyane, is a 3.3 km waymarked loop, about 1 h 20, on the Mahury heights. It runs between the Rorota lakes, Crique Angélique and the Loyola trail, through tropical forest.

Panels tell the story of human settlement here: long after Europeans arrived on the coast, Amerindians kept using the resources of Mount Mahury and Cayenne island. A viewpoint opens over the Rorota lakes, sometimes hidden by vegetation.
Two possible starts: from the Rorota trail or from the Loyola trail. The three trails combine into a full morning on the Mahury.

faq.q: How long is the Topu trail?
faq.a: 3.3 km, about 1 h 20.
From the Rorota trail or from the Loyola trail.
The Collectivité territoriale de Guyane.

p: On 21 March 1964, in Cayenne, General de Gaulle announced that the space centre would be built in French Guiana. Kourou was chosen for its closeness to the equator, its distance from hurricanes and earthquakes, and its low population. Four years later, on 9 April 1968, the Véronique sounding rocket opened the series of launches. Ariane 1 followed on 24 December 1979.
Now Europe's spaceport, the centre covers about 660 km². Testimonies from the families who were expropriated open the Guyaspace Expérience tour.

The guided bus tour visits the Ariane 6 and Vega-C launch facilities; it is free on booking, with ID. The Space Museum, with an entry fee, tells the space story in a playful way, with a planetarium and children's activities.
Book well ahead, especially in holiday periods. CNES also opens free viewing sites on launch days, on booking: check Karbé's Events tab.

faq.q: Is the space centre tour free?
faq.a: Yes, the guided site tour is free on booking, with ID. The Space Museum charges admission.

faq.q: Since when have rockets launched from Kourou?
faq.a: Since 9 April 1968, with the Véronique sounding rocket.
Yes, from viewing sites open on booking or from public places such as Kourou beach.

p: At the end of Pointe des Roches, the Dreyfus Tower is one of the few remains of Kourou's former agricultural penitentiary. Opened in 1856, it served as a semaphore to communicate with the penal colony on the Salvation Islands. After the penitentiary closed, most buildings were demolished for the Hôtel des Roches.

Pointe des Roches marks where the Kourou River meets the ocean. Its rocks, granodiorites crossed by pegmatite veins, are more than two billion years old. Near the old penal colony landing stage, it is also a birdwatching spot well known to local ornithologists.
The seafront is one of the public places to watch a launch: arrive early, crowds are big on launch nights. On launch days, some areas of Kourou and the islands are closed.

faq.a: A former semaphore of the Kourou penitentiary, opened in 1856, which signalled to the Salvation Islands.

faq.q: Can I watch a launch from the beach?
faq.a: Yes, Kourou's seafront is one of the public viewing sites.
Plage des Roches is one of Kourou's monitored bathing sites: follow the signs on site.

p: From the start of transportation in 1852, the Salvation Islands were given over to the penal colony, and remained so until the 1950s. Each island had its role: Île Royale held the convicts, Saint-Joseph was for solitary confinement, in silence and darkness, and Devil's Island received political deportees. Captain Alfred Dreyfus was held there from 1895 to 1899.
Owned by CNES since 1971, the archipelago is a viewing post for launches. With about 50,000 visitors in 2017, it is French Guiana's top tourist site.

Three volcanic islands about fifteen kilometres off Kourou. On Île Royale and Saint-Joseph you walk past the hospital, church, lighthouse and convict quarters, among coconut palms, monkeys and agoutis. Some penal colony buildings have been turned into accommodation.
Devil's Island cannot be visited: landing is forbidden. The islands close on some launch days; check Events before booking the crossing.

faq.a: No, landing is forbidden. You can visit Île Royale and Île Saint-Joseph.
CNES, since 1971.
Yes, from 1895 to 1899.

p: Founded in 1983 as a hummingbird breeding centre and turned into a zoo in 1985, the park closed in 2007 because it no longer met standards. It was taken over by the founders of the Balata garden in Martinique and reopened in 2008 as the Zoo de Guyane.

More than 450 animals of Guianese and Amazonian wildlife, in enclosures set in the forest: jaguar, tapir, giant otter, harpy eagle, emerald boa, anaconda. Raised walkways let you watch tree-dwelling species at canopy level. The site also hosts a wildlife care centre run by SOS Faune Sauvage Antilles-Guyane.
The zoo is on route du Galion, between Macouria and Montsinéry, about 25 to 40 minutes from Cayenne. It opens Wednesday to Sunday; come in the cool of the morning, when animals are active.

faq.a: Wednesday to Sunday; check hours and prices on its website before you go.
Mostly Guianese wildlife: jaguar, tapir, giant otter, harpy eagle, snakes.
Yes, a wildlife care centre is based there.

p: In 1931, the administration brought Indochinese prisoners, then called "Annamites", to French Guiana: about a hundred political prisoners and more than 400 common-law convicts. They were meant to serve as labour to develop the Inini territory. Camp Crique Anguille, in Montsinéry-Tonnegrande, operated from 1931 to 6 December 1944. Mortality there was high.

The remains of the camp, swallowed by the forest: walls, cells, foundations. The site of the Annamites penal colony and Crique Anguille has been a listed historic monument since 8 July 2022; it receives nearly 30,000 visitors a year.

A waymarked trail of about 5 km return, without major difficulty, starts from the Montsinéry road, about twenty kilometres from Cayenne; allow 2 to 3 hours. You can also reach the site by canoe up Crique Anguille. This is a place of memory: respect the remains.

faq.a: Indochinese prisoners, political and common-law, sent to French Guiana from 1931.
About 2 to 3 hours for the trail of about 5 km return.
Yes, it has been a listed historic monument since 2022.

p: The Grand Pripri de Yiyi covers nearly 15,000 hectares of marshes, mangroves and flooded savannas between the Sinnamary and Iracoubo rivers. Owned by the Conservatoire du littoral, it is co-managed with the town of Sinnamary and SEPANGUY, French Guiana's oldest nature conservation association. Since 2008 it has been a Ramsar wetland of international importance, under the name Sinnamary river estuary.

A 2.5 km trail crosses the marshes, with a tower and observation hides. You may see spectacled caimans, capybaras, squirrel monkeys, scarlet ibis and many waterbirds; with great luck, the giant otter.
The Maison de la Nature, on the RN1 about twelve kilometres from Sinnamary, is the gateway: exhibits, trail conditions, guided outings. Come early in the morning or late in the day.

faq.a: A freshwater marsh of the Guianese coastal plain.
2.5 km, about 1 h 30.
Early morning or late afternoon, when animals are most active.

p: The Saint-Joseph church in Iracoubo was built between 1887 and 1893, on the initiative of parish priest Prosper Raffray. In 1891 he met Pierre Huguet, a Parisian decorator sentenced to the penal colony and assigned to work on colonial road no. 1. Tradition credits him with the painted decoration, finished for the church's consecration on 6 January 1893. A few weeks later, on 20 February 1893, Huguet escaped.

Ceiling, choir, nave and pillars: about 600 m² of painted surfaces, in a naive, colourful style, following an iconography set by Raffray. It is sometimes nicknamed the "Sistine Chapel of the Amazon". The church has been a listed historic monument since 1978.
On the way out of the village towards Saint-Laurent, a memorial honours the 47 Kali'na and Arawak people taken to Europe in 1882 and 1892 to be exhibited in "human zoos".
An ideal stop on the Cayenne – Saint-Laurent road. Opening hours may vary: ask at the town hall if the church is closed.

faq.a: Tradition credits the convict Pierre Huguet, between 1891 and 1893.
About 600 m²: ceiling, choir, nave and pillars.
Yes, a listed historic monument since 1978.

p: Montagne des Singes rises to 161 metres south-west of Kourou. The land belongs to CNES and the ONF laid out the trails. Two routes: an easy botanical trail of about 650 m, and a longer loop of about 3.9 km, more demanding, that crosses a clearing, a creek and swamp forest before the summit.

At the top, the ONF shelter looks over the canopy, the town of Kourou, its river, the Salvation Islands and the space centre facilities; it also serves as a launch viewing point. In the forest, blue morphos and the calls of screaming pihas; golden-handed tamarins sometimes appear, monkeys are rare.

From the RN1 towards Saint-Laurent, turn left towards "Montagne des Singes / Dégrad Saramaka", then drive about 8 km to the car park. It climbs, and the path is slippery after rain: good shoes and water.

faq.a: About 3.9 km for the long loop, 650 m for the botanical trail.
Rarely: you are more likely to see blue morphos and birds.

faq.q: Can I watch a launch from there?
faq.a: Yes, the summit shelter serves as a viewing point.

p: Kourou has three lakes: Bois Diable, Marie-Claire and Bois Chaudat. Lake Bois Diable, in town, is one of Kourou's listed bathing sites along with Pollux, Castor and des Roches beaches. It is the freshwater option when the sea is rough or too muddy.

Water quality is monitored during the season, but in 2026 no result had been published for this site when we checked: look at the signs on site before swimming, and do not swim if it is forbidden. As anywhere in fresh water, avoid swimming with an open wound.

faq.q: Can I swim in Lake Bois Diable?
faq.a: It is a listed bathing site; check the water quality notice before you go.
In town, in Kourou.

faq.q: Are there other lakes in Kourou?
faq.a: Yes: Marie-Claire and Bois Chaudat.

p: French Guiana was a penal colony from 1852 to 1953. After heavy mortality in the first camps in the east, the penal colony moved west in 1857, and Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni was officially inaugurated on 21 January 1858. The Transportation Camp became the entry point for every convict sent from mainland France: more than 50,000 passed through its gate. It closed in 1948, and the town later acquired it.

The entrance gate, the yard, the cell blocks and the solitary confinement wing, including the cell attributed to Henri Charrière, known as Papillon. Saint-Laurent has been a Town of Art and History since 2007; its heritage interpretation centre (CIAP) occupies several blocks of the camp, with a permanent exhibition on the penal colony and the birth of the town.
Take the guided tour: it opens buildings closed to free visitors and gives the place its full meaning. Allow 1 to 1 h 30. Hours vary: ask at the tourist office or the CIAP.

faq.q: How many convicts passed through the camp?
faq.a: More than 50,000.

faq.q: Is the guided tour worth it?
faq.a: Yes: it gives access to extra buildings, including the solitary confinement wing.
In 1948; the Guianese penal colony ended for good in 1953.

p: The law of 27 May 1885 on the relegation of repeat offenders imposed life internment in a colony on habitual offenders, often guilty of petty crimes. The first relégués arrived in Saint-Jean-du-Maroni on 20 June 1887: nothing was ready, and they had to build the camp themselves. Nearly 17,000 relégués were sent to French Guiana until 1953, put to forced labour in the Saint-Jean penitentiary and its sub-camps.
The penitentiary buildings, on the bank of the Maroni, a few kilometres upstream from Saint-Laurent. The site is less known than the Transportation Camp, and quieter.
Visits are by appointment, on certain days only: ask at the Saint-Laurent tourist office. During European Heritage Days, combined tours of both camps sometimes include a pirogue ride.

faq.a: A repeat offender sentenced, on top of their sentence, to life internment in a colony under the 1885 law.

faq.q: How many relégués were there in French Guiana?
faq.a: Nearly 17,000, between 1887 and 1953.
No, by appointment through the Saint-Laurent tourist office.

p: The Maroni runs more than 520 km from the Tumuc-Humac mountains to the Atlantic and separates French Guiana from Suriname. It is France's fifth-longest land border, drawn in 1915 along the river's median line. But the Maroni is above all a living basin: opposite Saint-Laurent, the Surinamese town of Albina lives to the same rhythm.

The constant dance of pirogues: more than 1,000 crossings a day between the banks, and hundreds of children who travel to school in Saint-Laurent by river every morning. Pirogues also offer trips upstream, the gateway to the Maroni villages.
The official ferry links Saint-Laurent and Albina. Before crossing into Suriname, check the current formalities and border rules. Sunset over the river is worth the stop.

faq.a: More than 520 km, from the Tumuc-Humac mountains to the ocean.
Yes, by ferry or pirogue; check the required documents first.
More than 1,000 a day, according to estimates.

p: Javouhey was founded in 1978 as the second settlement for Hmong refugees from Laos in French Guiana, after Cacao. It stands on a former agricultural colony of Anne-Marie Javouhey, whose name it bears, in the commune of Mana. It has about a thousand inhabitants and lives from farming.
The Sunday morning market fills the central square: fruit and vegetables from the fields, embroidery, Hmong soup, spring rolls and sticky rice. The village is said to be more traditional than Cacao.
Come early on Sunday morning. Combine it with Mana and Les Hattes beach on the same weekend.

faq.a: Sunday morning.

faq.q: How does it differ from Cacao?
faq.a: Javouhey, founded in 1978, is said to be more traditional; Cacao is more touristy.
In the commune of Mana, in western French Guiana.

p: Mana was founded on 16 August 1828 by Mother Anne-Marie Javouhey, founder of the Sisters of Saint Joseph of Cluny, who drew the town's plans herself. The colony was then independent of Cayenne, which allowed her to educate and train enslaved people; the government entrusted her with preparing several hundred of them for freedom. She left French Guiana in 1843 and was beatified in 1950.
The Saint-Joseph church and its presbytery, listed historic monuments, Sister Javouhey's house, labelled "Maison des Illustres", and the old houses along the Mana River.
Mana is on the road to Awala-Yalimapo, about twenty kilometres from Les Hattes beach, and next to the Hmong village of Javouhey.

faq.a: Mother Anne-Marie Javouhey, in 1828.
The Saint-Joseph church, Sister Javouhey's house and the banks of the Mana River.

faq.q: Is it far from Les Hattes?
faq.a: About twenty kilometres.

p: Les Hattes beach, in Awala-Yalimapo, on Kali'na land, has historically been one of the world's largest leatherback nesting sites. The Amana national nature reserve was created in 1998 to protect them. Green turtles nest here too, with more than a thousand nests a year.

Leatherbacks have declined by about 97% on this beach, according to the Kwata association. Egg poaching, dogs and erosion threaten the nests. Since 2023, a natural hatchery, Kawana, run by Kwata with the reserve and customary chiefs, receives relocated nests at the eastern end of the beach.

Nesting is mainly from March to July. Follow the rules strictly: no white light, no flash, keep your distance. The Kali'na village welcomes you: respect the place. The reserve's visitor centre has an exhibition on turtles.

faq.q: When can I see turtles at Les Hattes?
faq.a: Mainly from March to July for nesting.
No: their numbers have fallen by about 97% on this beach. A hatchery has protected nests since 2023.
Kwata and the reserve organise visits and group sessions.

p: The Voltaire Falls, on the creek of the same name, a tributary of the Sparouine, are among the highest in French Guiana: a drop of about 35 metres. The catchment and the falls are protected as a landscape, and the area is listed as a natural area of ecological interest (ZNIEFF). The rocks, orthogneiss crossed by pegmatite veins, also interest geologists.

From Saint-Laurent, the laterite Paul Isnard track runs south for about 70 km to the Voltaire lodge; from there, allow 1 to 1 h 30 on foot. The territorial authority has run a programme to restore the site, with signposting from Saint-Laurent.
A 4x4 is recommended, as the track deteriorates in the rainy season. Plan the whole day, or a night in a hammock on site. No phone signal: leave your route and return time with someone.

faq.q: How high are the Voltaire Falls?
faq.a: About 35 metres.
Via the Paul Isnard track (about 70 km from Saint-Laurent), then on foot.
It is recommended, especially in the rainy season.

p: Saint-Laurent's central market, a few streets from the river, is the big market of western French Guiana. On market days, stalls of fruit, vegetables, couac and spices go up at dawn, next to food from the Maroni kitchens.
The main days are Wednesday and Saturday mornings, to be confirmed locally. Come early, before the heat, and bring cash. It is a good stop before or after visiting the Transportation Camp.

faq.q: Which days is Saint-Laurent market held?
faq.a: Mainly Wednesday and Saturday mornings; check locally.
